title: حِكَايَةُ الْمَلِكِ عُمَرَ بْنِ النُّعْمَانِ
part: Night 65 · King ʿUmar ibn al-Nuʿmān, continued
source: William Hay Macnaghten, ed., The Alif Laila, or Book of the Thousand Nights and One Night, vol. 1, Calcutta 1839 (“Calcutta II”), printed pp. 437–439 (Night 65, continuing directly from nights-64), transcribed from the 300 ppi scan (archive.org aliflailaorbooko01macn) by the editors' own transcription. The edition prints the prose essentially unpointed: ALL VOCALIZATION (tashkīl) IS EDITORIAL — ours, not the edition's — and the alphabet button strips it back to the bare rasm exactly as Macnaghten prints it. Romanization is simplified IJMES. Spelling, including the edition's Middle Arabic forms and its occasional compositor's slips, is preserved unaltered; a few genuinely obscure or corrupt-looking forms are vocalized by evident sense and flagged in the notes rather than silently repaired. Read-aloud audio is a Modern Standard Arabic reading of this vocalised text, synthesized by machine, with word-by-word timing generated the same way.
about: Night 65 continues the tale of King ʿUmar ibn al-Nuʿmān. Nuzhat al-Zamān goes on with her anecdotes of the caliph ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz: his image of the river of the caliphate, which the Umayyads drained; his refusal to enrich his sons from the public treasury; dreams of the dead; the wolves that keep peace among the flock under a just ruler; his sermon from a clay pulpit; and his swoon as his wife Fāṭima weeps over him. The night closes the second section of the first chapter of her discourse. As with every printed edition of the Nights, this one belongs to the late Egyptian recension (ZER) — an eighteenth-century expansion padded out to a literal 1001 nights; no printed edition is a medieval text, and Macnaghten regularised the language here and there, so some Middle Arabic texture is a nineteenth-century retrofit.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا كَانَتِ اللَّيْلَةُ الْخَامِسَةُ وَالسِّتُّونَ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā kānati al-laylatu al-khāmisatu wa-al-sittūna
sentences.l: And when it was the night, the fifth and the sixty,
sentences.i: And when it was the sixty-fifth night,

sentences.t: قَاتْ بَلَغَنِي أَيُّهَا الْمَلِكُ السَّعِيدُأَنَّ نُرْهَةَ الزَّمَانِ قَالَتْ فَقَالَ عُمَرُ بْنُ عَبْدِ الْعَزِيزِ إِنَّ اللَّهَ بَعَثَ مُحَمَّدًا صَلَّى اللَّهُ عَلَيْهِ وَسَلَّمَ رَحْمَةً لِنَاسٍ وَعَذَابًا عَلَى آخَرِينَ ثُمَّ اخْتَارَ لَهُ مَا عِنْدَهُ فَقَبَضَهُ إِلَيْهِ وَتَرَكَ لَهُمْ نَهْرًا يَشْرَبُونَ مِنْهُ
sentences.tr: qāt balaghanī ayyuhā al-maliku al-saʿīdu anna Nurhata al-Zamāni qālat fa-qāla ʿUmaru ibnu ʿAbdi al-ʿAzīzi inna Allāha baʿatha Muḥammadan ṣallā Allāhu ʿalayhi wa-sallama raḥmatan li-nāsin wa-ʿadhāban ʿalā ākharīna thumma ikhtāra lahu mā ʿindahu fa-qabaḍahu ilayhi wa-taraka lahum nahran yashrabūna minhu
sentences.l: She said (the print: “she-said” without its l): It has reached me, O king the fortunate, that Nuzhat al-Zamān said: And ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz said: Truly God sent Muḥammad, God bless him and give him peace, as a mercy for people and a punishment upon others; then He chose for him what is with Him, and took him to Himself, and left them a river from which they drink.
sentences.i: She said: It has reached me, O fortunate king, that Nuzhat al-Zamān said: ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz said, “God sent Muḥammad, God bless him and grant him peace, as a mercy to some people and a punishment to others; then He chose for him what is with Him and took him to Himself, and left them a river to drink from.”
sentences.n: The print drops the lām of قالت (“she said”) and gives قات, runs السعيد and أن together, and misprints نزهة as نرهة; all are kept as printed and read as qālat, al-saʿīdu anna and Nuzhat. “Mercy for people” is printed without the article (لناس), as the edition has it. The river is ʿUmar's image for the caliphate and its fair rule.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ قَامَ أَبُو بَكْرٍ الصِّدِّيقُ خَلِيفَةً بَعْدَهُ فَتَرَكَ النَّهْرَ عَلَى حَالِهِ وَعَمِلَ مَا يُرْضِى اللَّهَ ثُمَّ قَامَ عُمَرُ قَائِمًا فَعَمِلَ عَمَلًا وَاجْتَهَدَ اجْتِهَادًا مَا يَقْدِرُ أَحَدٌ عَلَى مِثْلِهِ
sentences.tr: thumma qāma Abū Bakrin al-Ṣiddīqu khalīfatan baʿdahu fa-taraka al-nahra ʿalā ḥālihi wa-ʿamila mā yurḍī Allāha thumma qāma ʿUmaru qāʾiman fa-ʿamila ʿamalan wa-ijtahada ijtihādan mā yaqdiru aḥadun ʿalā mithlihi
sentences.l: Then rose Abū Bakr the truthful, a caliph after him, and left the river on its state and did what pleases God; then rose ʿUmar, standing, and did a deed and strove a striving that no one is able to the like of.
sentences.i: Then Abū Bakr the Truthful rose as caliph after him, left the river as it was, and did what pleases God. Then ʿUmar rose and worked and strove as no one else could.
sentences.n: “Rose” (qāma) is the idiom for taking up the office. ʿUmar here is ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb, the second caliph.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا قَامَ عُثْمَانُ اشْتَقَّ مِنَ النَّهْرِ نَهْرًا ثُمَّ وَلِيَ مُعْوِبَةُ فَاشْتَقَّ الْأَنْهَارَ مِنْهُ ثُمَّ لَمْ يَزَلْ كَذَلِكَ يَشْتَقُّ مِنْهُ يَزِيدُ وَبَنُو مَرْوَانَ كَعَبْدِ الْمَلِكِ وَالْوَلِيدِ وَسُلَيْمَانَ وَيَبِسَ النَّهْرُ الْأَعْظَمُ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā qāma ʿUthmānu ishtaqqa mina al-nahri nahran thumma waliya Muʿwibatu fa-ishtaqqa al-anhāra minhu thumma lam yazal kadhālika yashtaqqu minhu Yazīdu wa-banū Marwāna ka-ʿAbdi al-Maliki wa-al-Walīdi wa-Sulaymāna wa-yabisa al-nahru al-aʿẓamu
sentences.l: And when ʿUthmān rose, he split from the river a river; then Muʿwiba took charge and split the rivers from it; then it did not cease so, Yazīd and the sons-of-Marwān splitting from it, like ʿAbd al-Malik and al-Walīd and Sulaymān; and the greatest river dried up.
sentences.i: When ʿUthmān took office he cut a channel from the river. Then Muʿāwiya took charge and cut more channels from it, and so it went on, with Yazīd and the house of Marwān, ʿAbd al-Malik, al-Walīd and Sulaymān, each drawing from it, until the great river itself ran dry.
sentences.n: The print gives معوبة, a misprint for Muʿāwiya (معاوية); it is kept as printed. Channels cut from the river stand for the revenues and powers the Umayyads drew away from the common treasury.

sentences.t: حَتَّى آلَ الْأَمْرُ إِلَّيَّ فَأَحْبَبْتُ أَنْ أَرُدَّ النَّهْرَ إِلَى مَا كَانَ عَلَيْهِ
sentences.tr: ḥattā āla al-amru illayya fa-aḥbabtu an arudda al-nahra ilā mā kāna ʿalayhi
sentences.l: Until the matter reverted to me, and I loved that I return the river to what it was upon.
sentences.i: Until the matter came to me, and I wished to restore the river to what it had been.
sentences.n: The print puts the shadda of إلي on the lām (الّي) rather than the yā; it is kept in that place, and the word is read ilayya, “to me”.

sentences.t: فَقَالَتْ قَدْ أَرَدْتُ كَلَامَكَ وَمُذَاكَرَتَكَ فَقَطْ فَإِنْ كَانَتْ هَذِهِ مَقَالَتَكَ فَلَسْتُ بِذَاكِرَةٍ لَكَ شَئْاً
sentences.tr: fa-qālat qad aradtu kalāmaka wa-mudhākarataka faqaṭ fa-in kānat hādhihi maqālataka fa-lastu bi-dhākiratin laka shayʾan
sentences.l: And she said: I only wanted your speech and conversing with you; and if this is your saying, then I am not a mentioner to you of anything.
sentences.i: Then she said, “I only wanted to speak and talk with you. If this is how you speak, I will bring up nothing more to you.”
sentences.n: The speaker is ʿUmar's aunt, who has come to plead with him at the end of the previous night. In فَلَسْتُ بِذَاكِرَةٍ the بِـ only strengthens the negated predicate. The print has شيا, read shayʾan, “anything”.

sentences.t: وَرَجَعْتُ إِلَى بَنِي أُمَيَّةَ فَقُلْتُ لَهُمْ ذُوقُوا عَاقِبَةَ أَمْرِكُمْ بِتَزْوِيجِكُمْ إِلَى عُمَرَ
sentences.tr: wa-rajaʿtu ilā banī Umayyata fa-qultu lahum dhūqū ʿāqibata amrikum bi-tazwījikum ilā ʿUmara
sentences.l: And I returned to the sons-of-Umayya and said to them: Taste the outcome of your affair, by your marrying-off to ʿUmar.
sentences.i: And I went back to the Banū Umayya and said to them, “Taste the result of what you did, in giving a bride to ʿUmar.”
sentences.n: She means the Umayyads' choice to marry one of their own into ʿUmar's house; the idiom is تَزْوِيجٌ إِلَى فُلَانٍ, “to give in marriage to so-and-so”.

sentences.t: وَقِيلَ لَمَّا حَضَرَتْ عُمَرَ بْنَ عَبْدِ الْعَزِيزِ الْوَفَاةُ جَمَعَ أَوْلَادَهُ حَوْلَهُ
sentences.tr: wa-qīla lammā ḥaḍarat ʿUmara ibna ʿAbdi al-ʿAzīzi al-wafātu jamaʿa awlādahu ḥawlahu
sentences.l: And it was said: When death attended ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz, he gathered his sons around him.
sentences.i: It is told that when death came to ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz, he gathered his sons around him.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ لَهُ مَسْلَمَةُ بْنُ عَبْدِ الْمَلِكِ يَا أَمِيرَ الْمُؤْمِنِينَ كَيْفَ تَتْرُكُ أَوْلَادَكَ فُقَرَاءَ وَأَنْتَ رَاعِيهِمْ فَمَا يَمْنَعُكَ أَحَدٌ فِي حَيٰوتِكَ مِنْ أَنْ تُعْطِيَهُمْ مِنْ بَيْتِ الْمَالِ مَا يُغْنِيهِمْ وَهَذَا أَوْلَى مِنْ أَنْ تَرْجِعَهُ إِلَى الْوَالِى بِعَدْلٍ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla lahu Maslamatu ibnu ʿAbdi al-Maliki yā amīra al-muʾminīna kayfa taturku awlādaka fuqarāʾa wa-anta rāʿīhim fa-mā yamnaʿuka aḥadun fī ḥayātika min an tuʿṭiyahum min bayti al-māli mā yughnīhim wa-hādhā awlā min an tarjiʿahu ilā al-wālī bi-ʿadlin
sentences.l: And Maslama ibn ʿAbd al-Malik said to him: O commander of the believers, how do you leave your sons poor, and you their shepherd? No one hinders you in your life from giving them, from the house of the wealth, what enriches them; and this is more fitting than that you return it to the governor with justice.
sentences.i: Maslama ibn ʿAbd al-Malik said to him, “Commander of the Faithful, how can you leave your sons poor when you are their shepherd? No one prevents you, while you live, from giving them from the public treasury enough to make them rich, and that is better than handing it back to the next ruler to deal with justly.”
sentences.n: حيوتك is the print's spelling of حياتك, “your life”, with the dagger alif. Maslama, a brother of the earlier caliph Sulaymān, speaks for the Umayyad family. The last clause is compressed: the treasury would pass to the next governor, who is expected to rule justly.

sentences.t: فَنَظَرَ إِلَى مَسْلَمَةَ نَظَرَ مُغْضَبٍ مُتَعَجِّبٍ ثُمَّ قَالَ يَا مَسْلَمَةُ مَنَعْتُهُمْ أَيَّامَ حَيٰوتِي فَكَيْفَ أَشْقَى بِهِمْ بَعْدَ مَمَاتِي إِنَّ أَوْلَادِي مَا بَيْنَ رَجُلَيْنِ إِمَّا مُطِيعٌ لِلَّهِ تَعَالَى فَاللَّهُ يُصْلِحُ شَأْنَهُ أَوْ عَاصٍ فَمَا كُنْتُ لِأَنْ أُعِينَهُ عَلَى مَعْصِيَةٍ
sentences.tr: fa-naẓara ilā Maslamata naẓara mughḍabin mutaʿajjibin thumma qāla yā Maslamatu manaʿtuhum ayyāma ḥayātī fa-kayfa ashqā bihim baʿda mamātī inna awlādī mā bayna rajulayni immā muṭīʿun li-Allāhi taʿālā fa-Allāhu yuṣliḥu shaʾnahu aw ʿāṣin fa-mā kuntu li-an uʿīnahu ʿalā maʿṣiyatin
sentences.l: And he looked at Maslama, the look of one angered, amazed, then said: O Maslama, I withheld them in the days of my life, so how shall I be wretched through them after my death? Truly my sons are between two men: either obedient to God the exalted, and God sets right his state; or disobedient, and I would not be one to help him in disobedience.
sentences.i: He looked at Maslama like a man both angry and astonished, and said, “Maslama, I kept it from them all my life; why should I be made wretched on their account after my death? My sons are one of two kinds: either obedient to God Most High, and God will set his affairs right, or disobedient, and I will not be the one to help him in disobedience.”
sentences.n: حيوتي is the print's spelling of حياتي; the dagger alif supplies the long ā.

sentences.t: يَا مَسْلَمَةُ إِنِّي حَضَرْتُ وَإِيَّاكَ حِينَ دُفِنَ بَعْضُ بَنِي مَرْوَانَ فَحَمَلَتْنِي عَيْنِي عِنْدَهُ فَرَأَيْتُهُ فِى الْمَنَامِ أُقْضِيَ إِلَى أَمْرٍ مِنْ أُمُورِ اللَّهِ عَزَّ وَجَلَّ فَهَالَنِي وَرَاعَنِي فَعَاهَدْتُ اللَّهَ أَنْ لَا أَعْمَلَ عَمَلَهُ إِنْ وُلِّيتُ وَقَدِ اجْتَهَدْتُ فِي ذَلِكَ مُدَّةَ حَيٰوتِي
sentences.tr: yā Maslamatu innī ḥaḍartu wa-iyyāka ḥīna dufina baʿḍu banī Marwāna fa-ḥamalatnī ʿaynī ʿindahu fa-raʾaytuhu fī al-manāmi uqḍiya ilā amrin min umūri Allāhi ʿazza wa-jalla fa-hālanī wa-rāʿanī fa-ʿāhadtu Allāha an lā aʿmala ʿamalahu in wuliytu wa-qadi ijtahadtu fī dhālika muddata ḥayātī
sentences.l: O Maslama, I was present, and you, when one of the sons-of-Marwān was buried, and my eye carried me by his grave, and I saw him in the sleep, brought to a matter of the matters of God, mighty and majestic; and it terrified me and alarmed me, and I made a covenant with God that I would not do his deed if I were made ruler; and I have striven in that for the span of my life.
sentences.i: Maslama, you and I were present when one of the Banū Marwān was buried, and sleep overcame me beside his grave. In my dream I saw him brought before one of the matters of God, mighty and glorious, and it terrified and appalled me. So I made a covenant with God that I would not do what he did if I were ever given power, and I have striven at that all my life.
sentences.n: Printed اقضي, with qāf, is read as a passive, “was brought to”; the edition may mean افضي (fāʾ), “came to”, with much the same sense. “His deed” is whatever the dead Umayyad had done in office, which the dream showed to be weighed against him. حيوتي: the print's spelling of حياتي.

sentences.t: وَأَرْجُوأَنْ أُقْضَى إِلَى عَفْوِ رَبِّي
sentences.tr: wa-arjū an uqḍā ilā ʿafwi rabbī
sentences.l: And I hope that I be brought to the pardon of my Lord.
sentences.i: And I hope to be brought to my Lord's pardon.
sentences.n: The print joins وارجوان into one word (wa-arjū an) and again has اقضى with qāf, here read as a passive, “be brought to”.

sentences.t: قَالَ مَسْلَمَةُ تُوُفِّيَ رَجُلٌ حَضَرْتُ دَفْنَهُ فَلَمَّا فَرَغْتُ مِنْ دَفْنِهِ حَمَلَتْنِي عَيْنِي فَرَأَيْتُهُ فِيمَا يَرَى النَّائِمُ فِي رَوْضَةٍ فِيهَا أَنْهَارٌ جَارِيَةٌ وَعَلَيْهِ ثِيَابٌ بِيضٌ فَأَقْبَلَ عَلَيَّ وَقَالَ يَا مَسْلَمَةُ لِمِثْلِ هَذَا فَلْيَعْمَلِ الْعَامِلُونَ وَنَحْوُ هَذَا كَثِيرٌ
sentences.tr: qāla Maslamatu tuwuffiya rajulun ḥaḍartu dafnahu fa-lammā faraghtu min dafnihi ḥamalatnī ʿaynī fa-raʾaytuhu fīmā yarā al-nāʾimu fī rawḍatin fīhā anhārun jāriyatun wa-ʿalayhi thiyābun bīḍun fa-aqbala ʿalayya wa-qāla yā Maslamatu li-mithli hādhā fa-li-yaʿmali al-ʿāmilūna wa-naḥwu hādhā kathīrun
sentences.l: Maslama said: A man died whose burial I attended, and when I finished his burial my eye carried me, and I saw him as the sleeper sees, in a garden in which were running rivers, and upon him white garments; and he turned to me and said: O Maslama, for the like of this let the workers work! And the like of this is much.
sentences.i: Maslama said, “A man died whose burial I attended. When I had finished burying him, sleep overcame me, and I saw him in a dream in a garden with running streams, dressed in white. He turned to me and said, ‘Maslama, for the like of this let those who work, work!’ There are many tales like this.”
sentences.n: “For the like of this let the workers work” echoes the Qurʾān (37:61). The closing words are the storyteller's own aside, not Maslama's.

sentences.t: وَقَالَ بَعْضُ الثِّقَاتِ كُنْتُ أَحْلُبُ الْغَنَمَ فِي خِلَافَةِ عُمَرَ بْنِ عَبْدِ الْعَزِيزِ فَمَرَرْتُ بِرَاعٍ فَرَأَيْتُ مَعَ غَنَمِهِ ذِئْبًا أَوْ ذِئَابًا فَظَنَّتُ أَنَّهَا كِلَابُهَا وَلَمْ أَكُنْ رَأَيْتُ الذِّئَابَ قَبْلَ ذَلِكَ فَقُلْتُ مَا تَصْنَعُ بِهَذِهِ الْكِلَابِ فَقَالَ إِنَّهَا لَيْسَتْ كِلَابًا بَلْ هِيَ ذِئَابٌ فَقُلْتُ هَلْ ذِئَابٌ فِي غَنَمٍ لَمْ تَضُرَّهَا فَقَالَ إِذَا صَلَحَ الرَّأْسُ صَلَحَ الْجَسَدُ
sentences.tr: wa-qāla baʿḍu al-thiqāti kuntu aḥlubu al-ghanama fī khilāfati ʿUmara ibni ʿAbdi al-ʿAzīzi fa-marartu bi-rāʿin fa-raʾaytu maʿa ghanamihi dhiʾban aw dhiʾāban fa-ẓanattu annahā kilābuhā wa-lam akun raʾaytu al-dhiʾāba qabla dhālika fa-qultu mā taṣnaʿu bi-hādhihi al-kilābi fa-qāla innahā laysat kilāban bal hiya dhiʾābun fa-qultu hal dhiʾābun fī ghanamin lam taḍurrahā fa-qāla idhā ṣalaḥa al-raʾsu ṣalaḥa al-jasadu
sentences.l: And one of the trustworthy-ones said: I was milking the flock in the caliphate of ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz, and I passed by a herdsman and saw with his flock a wolf or wolves, and I supposed they were its dogs, for I had not seen wolves before that; so I said: What do you do with these dogs? And he said: They are not dogs, rather they are wolves. I said: Are there wolves among a flock that they do not harm? And he said: When the head is sound, the body is sound.
sentences.i: One of the reliable authorities said, “In the caliphate of ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz I used to milk sheep. I passed a shepherd and saw a wolf, or wolves, with his flock, and took them for his dogs, since I had never seen wolves before. I said, ‘What do you do with these dogs?’ He said, ‘They are not dogs; they are wolves.’ I said, ‘Wolves among a flock, and they do not hurt it?’ He said, ‘When the head is sound, the body is sound.’”
sentences.n: The print has فظنت where فظننت (“I supposed”) is meant, with one nūn dropped; it is written with a shadda and read ẓanantu. “The head” is the ruler: under a just caliph even wolves keep the peace. الثقات is the plural of ثقة, “a trusted transmitter”, the usual term for a reliable authority.

sentences.t: وَخَطَبَ عُمَرُ بْنُ عَبْدِ الْعَزِيزِ عَلَى مِنْبَرٍ مِنَ الطِّينِ فَحَمِدَ اللَّهَ تَعَالَى وَأَثْنَى عَلَيْهِ ثُمَّ تَكَلَّمَ بِثَلٰثِ كَلِمَاتٍ فَقَالَ
sentences.tr: wa-khaṭaba ʿUmaru ibnu ʿAbdi al-ʿAzīzi ʿalā minbarin mina al-ṭīni fa-ḥamida Allāha taʿālā wa-athnā ʿalayhi thumma takallama bi-thalāthi kalimātin fa-qāla
sentences.l: And ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz preached upon a pulpit of clay, and praised God the exalted and lauded Him, then spoke three words, and said:
sentences.i: ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz preached from a pulpit made of clay. He praised God Most High and extolled Him, then spoke three sentences, saying:
sentences.n: ثلث is the print's spelling of ثلاث, “three”, with the dagger alif. “Words” (kalimāt) here means short sayings.

sentences.t: أَيُّهَا النَّاسُ أَصْلِحُوا أَسْرَارَكُمْ لِتَصْلُحَ عَلَانِيَتُكُمْ لِإِخْوَانِكُمْ وَتُكْفَوْا أَمْرَ دُنْيَاكُمْ
sentences.tr: ayyuhā al-nāsu aṣliḥū asrārakum li-taṣluḥa ʿalāniyatukum li-ikhwānikum wa-tukfaw amra dunyākum
sentences.l: O people, set right your secrets so that your openness be sound for your brothers, and you be spared the matter of your world.
sentences.i: People, mend what you keep secret, so that what you do openly may be sound for your brothers, and you will be spared the cares of your worldly life.
sentences.n: For the lām of لِتَصْلُحَ, “so that”, with the subjunctive. In لِإِخْوَانِكُمْ the لِـ marks those for whom the public conduct is sound, “for your brothers”.

sentences.t: وَاعْلَمُوا أَنَّ الرَّجُلَ لَيْسَ بَيْنَهُ وَبَيْنَ آدَمَ رَجُلٌ حَيٌّ فِى الْمَوْتَى مَاتَ عَبْدُ الْمَلِكِ وَمَنْ قَبْلَهُ وَيَمُوتُ عُمَرُ وَمَنْ بَعْدَهُ
sentences.tr: wa-iʿlamū anna al-rajula laysa baynahu wa-bayna Ādama rajulun ḥayyun fī al-mawtā māta ʿAbdu al-Maliki wa-man qablahu wa-yamūtu ʿUmaru wa-man baʿdahu
sentences.l: And know that the man — there is not between him and Adam a living man among the dead: ʿAbd al-Malik died, and whoever was before him, and ʿUmar will die, and whoever is after him.
sentences.i: And know that between any man and Adam there is no one still living among the dead: ʿAbd al-Malik died, and all before him, and ʿUmar will die, and all after him.
sentences.n: The sentence is compressed: every one of the men between a person and Adam is dead. ʿAbd al-Malik, Maslama's father, was an earlier caliph and ʿUmar's uncle.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ لَهُ مَسْلَمَةُ يَا أَمِيرَ الْمُؤْمِنِينَ لَوْ عَمِلْنَا لَكَ مَنْكِئًا لِتَعْتَمِدَ عَلَيْهِ قَلِيلًا فَقَالَ أَخَافُ أَنْ يَكُونَ فِي عُنُقِي مِنْهُ إِثْمٌ يَوْمَ الْقِيَامَةِ ثُمَّ شَهَقَ شَهْقَةً فَخَرَّ مَغْشِيًّا عَلَيْهِ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla lahu Maslamatu yā amīra al-muʾminīna law ʿamilnā laka mankiʾan li-taʿtamida ʿalayhi qalīlan fa-qāla akhāfu an yakūna fī ʿunuqī minhu ithmun yawma al-qiyāmati thumma shahaqa shahqatan fa-kharra maghshiyyan ʿalayhi
sentences.l: And Maslama said to him: O commander of the believers, if we were to make for you a leaning-place, that you might lean on it a little! And he said: I fear that there be on my neck, from it, a sin on the day of the resurrection. Then he drew a sob, and fell down, swooning.
sentences.i: Maslama said to him, “Commander of the Faithful, if only we made you a cushion to lean on a little!” He said, “I fear that on the Day of Resurrection there would be a sin on my neck for it.” Then he gasped, and fell down in a faint.
sentences.n: The print gives منكئا; the sense is a support to lean on, the usual word being متكأ (“cushion”), and it is vocalised as printed. “On my neck” is the idiom for a burden of guilt one must answer for.

sentences.t: فَقَالَتْ فَاطِمَةُ يَامَرْيَمُ يَامُزَاحِمُ يَا فُلَانُ انْظُرُوا إِلَى هَذَا الرَّجُلِ فَجَاءَتْ فَاطِمَةُ تَصُبُّ عَلَيْهِ الْمَاءَ وَتَبْكِي حَتَّى أَفَاقَ مِنْ غَشْيَتِهِ
sentences.tr: fa-qālat Fāṭimatu yā Maryamu yā Muzāḥimu yā fulānu unẓurū ilā hādhā al-rajuli fa-jāʾat Fāṭimatu taṣubbu ʿalayhi al-māʾa wa-tabkī ḥattā afāqa min ghashyatihi
sentences.l: And Fāṭima said: O Maryam, O Muzāḥim, O so-and-so, look to this man! And Fāṭima came, pouring on him the water and weeping, until he recovered from his swoon.
sentences.i: Fāṭima cried, “Maryam! Muzāḥim! You there, look at this man!” Then Fāṭima came and poured water over him, weeping, until he came to from his faint.
sentences.n: The print writes يامريم and يامزاحم with the vocative particle joined to the name. Fāṭima is ʿUmar's wife, a daughter of the caliph ʿAbd al-Malik. Maryam and Muzāḥim are members of the household.

sentences.t: فَرَأَهَا تَبْكِي فَقَالَ مَا يُبْكِيكِ يَا فَاطِمَةُ قَالَتْ يَا أَمِيرَ الْمُؤْمِنِينَ رَأَبْتُ مَصْرَعَكَ بَيْنَ أَيْدِينَا فَتَذَكَّرْتُ مَصْرَعَكَ بَيْنَ يَدَىِ اللَّهِ تَعَالَى لِلْمَوْتِ وَتَخَلِّيكَ عَنِ الدُّنْيَا وَفِرَاقَكَ لَنَا فَذَاكَ الَّذِي أَبْكَانِي
sentences.tr: fa-raʾāhā tabkī fa-qāla mā yubkīki yā Fāṭimatu qālat yā amīra al-muʾminīna raʾabtu maṣraʿaka bayna aydīnā fa-tadhakkartu maṣraʿaka bayna yadayi Allāhi taʿālā li-al-mawti wa-takhallīka ʿani al-dunyā wa-firāqaka lanā fa-dhāka alladhī abkānī
sentences.l: And he saw her weeping and said: What makes you weep, O Fāṭima? She said: O commander of the believers, I saw your falling between our hands, and I remembered your falling between the hands of God the exalted for death, and your giving-up of the world and your parting from us; that is what made me weep.
sentences.i: He saw her weeping and said, “What makes you weep, Fāṭima?” She said, “Commander of the Faithful, I saw you fall before our eyes, and it reminded me of how you will fall before God Most High at death, and of your giving up the world and leaving us. That is what made me weep.”
sentences.n: The print gives رأبت for رأيت (“I saw”), a misprint of bāʾ for yāʾ; it is vocalised as printed and read raʾaytu. “Between the hands of” means “in the presence of”. بين أيدينا is “before us”.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ حَسْبُكِ يَا فَاطِمَةُ فَلَقَدْ أَبْلَغْتِ ثُمَّ قَامَ فَسَقَطَ فَضَمَّتْهُ فَاطِمَةُ إِلَيْهَا وَقَالَتْ بِأَبِي أَنْتَ وَأُمِّي يَا أَمِيرَ الْمُؤْمِنِينَ مَا نَسْتَطِيعُ أَنْ نُكَلِّمَكَ كُلُّنَا
sentences.tr: fa-qāla ḥasbuki yā Fāṭimatu fa-laqad ablaghti thumma qāma fa-saqaṭa fa-ḍammathu Fāṭimatu ilayhā wa-qālat bi-abī anta wa-ummī yā amīra al-muʾminīna mā nastaṭīʿu an nukallimaka kullunā
sentences.l: And he said: Enough for you, O Fāṭima; you have indeed reached-the-full. Then he rose and fell, and Fāṭima embraced him to her, and said: With my father you, and my mother, O commander of the believers! We are not able to speak to you, all of us.
sentences.i: He said, “Enough, Fāṭima; you have said all there is to say.” Then he rose and fell again, and Fāṭima held him to her and said, “May my father and mother be your ransom, Commander of the Faithful! We cannot speak to you, none of us.”
sentences.n: بِأَبِي أَنْتَ وَأُمِّي is the common oath of devotion, “my father and mother for you”. Here the بِـ means “in exchange for”, “as ransom for”. أَبْلَغْتِ: “you have conveyed it fully”.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ إِنَّ نُزْهَةَ الزَّمَانِ قَالَتْ لِأَخِيهَا شَرْكَانَ وَلِلْقُضَاةِ الْأَرْبَعَةِ تَتِمَّةَ الْفَصْلِ الثَّانِي مِنَ الْبَابِ الْأَوَّلِ
sentences.tr: thumma inna Nuzhata al-Zamāni qālat li-akhīhā Sharkāna wa-li-al-quḍāti al-arbaʿati tatimmata al-faṣli al-thānī mina al-bābi al-awwali
sentences.l: Then Nuzhat al-Zamān said to her brother Sharkān and to the four judges the completion of the second section of the first chapter.
sentences.i: Then Nuzhat al-Zamān told her brother Sharkān and the four judges the rest of the second section of the first chapter.
sentences.n: The print marks the close of the second section of the first chapter of her discourse. Nuzhat al-Zamān's discourse of exemplary anecdotes began in the nights before this one.

sentences.t: وَأَدْرَكَ شَهْرَ زَادَ الصَّبَاحُ فَسَكَتَتْ عَنِ الْكَلَامِ الْمُبَاحِ
sentences.tr: wa-adraka Shahrazāda al-ṣabāḥu fa-sakatat ʿani al-kalāmi al-mubāḥi
sentences.l: And the morning overtook Shahrazād, and she fell silent from the speech the permitted.
sentences.i: And the morning overtook Shahrazād, and she fell silent, leaving the permitted speech unspoken.
sentences.n: The stock close of a night. The print writes her name as two words, شهر زاد.
